questions.q: Define the three dimensions of colour (hue, value, intensity) and give one fabric example for each dimension where changing only that dimension alters the design effect.
questions.a: Hue is the colour name (e.g., red, blue-green) determined by wavelength; value is lightness/darkness (tint = hue + white, shade = hue + black); intensity/chroma is purity/saturation (high intensity = pure hue, low intensity = hue + complement or grey). Example: A cotton kurta in pure red (high intensity) vs. brick red (low intensity, greyed) changes the mood from festive to subdued without altering hue or value. A wrong answer (e.g., confusing value with intensity, or saying "tint adds black") reveals the student cannot isolate variables — a critical error when adjusting only one dimension in dyeing or printing.

questions.q: A student says: "Monochromatic and achromatic schemes are the same because both use only one colour." Explain why this is incorrect using the colour wheel and value scale.
questions.a: Monochromatic uses ONE hue varied in value (tints/shades) and/or intensity (e.g., navy, sky blue, pastel blue — all blue hue). Achromatic uses NO hue — only neutrals (black, white, greys) which have zero chroma. On the colour wheel, monochromatic stays on one spoke; achromatic occupies the centre axis. A wrong answer shows the student conflates "single colour family" with "no colour" — leading to design errors like calling a grey-and-white outfit "monochromatic blue" in board exams.

questions.q: A designer wants to create a salwar-kurta-dupatta set using a split-complementary scheme based on yellow-orange as the dominant hue. List the exact three hues she must use (by colour wheel position) and specify which should dominate, which should accent, and why.
questions.a: Split-complementary of yellow-orange (Y-O) uses Y-O + the two neighbours of its complement (blue-violet). Complement of Y-O is blue-violet (B-V); neighbours are blue (B) and violet (V). So the three hues: yellow-orange (dominant, 60%), blue (accent, 30%), violet (accent, 10%). Dominant covers largest area (kurta); accents in dupatta border/piping. Wrong answer (e.g., using blue-green instead of blue) shows inability to locate complements and neighbours on the wheel — a direct board-mark loss in scheme identification questions.

questions.q: Compare and contrast analogous and triadic schemes in terms of: (a) number of hues, (b) wheel positions, (c) visual energy, (d) difficulty in balancing for Indian skin tones. Give one garment example for each.
questions.a: Analogous: 2-3 adjacent hues (e.g., yellow, yellow-orange, orange), low contrast, harmonious/calm, easy to balance — example: autumn-toned lehenga-choli. Triadic: 3 hues equidistant (120° apart, e.g., red, yellow, blue), high contrast, vibrant/energetic, hard to balance without one dominating — example: primary-colour blocked Anarkali. Wrong answer (e.g., saying triadic uses adjacent hues) reveals confusion between "equidistant" and "neighbouring" — a frequent MCQ trap in CUET/Home Science entrance tests.

questions.q: Critique this design decision: "For a petite bride's wedding lehenga, I chose a double-complementary scheme (red-green + yellow-violet) in full-intensity hues with equal proportions." Judge its suitability using proportion, figure type, and colour psychology principles.
questions.a: Unsuitable. Double-complementary (4 hues) in full intensity creates visual vibration — overwhelming on a petite frame (violates proportion: equal divisions shorten height). Red-green is culturally auspicious but full-intensity equal proportions cause simultaneous contrast fatigue. Better: monochromatic red (tints/shades) with gold (accented neutral) to elongate silhouette. Wrong answer (e.g., "it's festive so it works") shows inability to evaluate schemes against figure/occasion — a competency-based board question pattern.

questions.q: Create a new 4-hue colour scheme for a summer resort-wear collection targeting Gen-Z buyers. Name it, specify the four hues by wheel position, assign value/intensity variations, and justify each choice using trend, climate, and psychology factors.
questions.a: Scheme: "Coastal Drift" — Hues: blue-green (BG), green (G), yellow-green (YG), yellow (Y) — an extended analogous (4 adjacent). Values: BG shade (deep lagoon, 20%), G tint (seafoam, 30%), YG tint (lime splash, 30%), Y tint (sunlit sand, 20%). Intensities: BG low (greyed), others medium-high. Justification: Adjacent hues = calm (vacation mood); cool-dominant suits Indian summer heat; yellow-green/yellow accents = Gen-Z "dopamine dressing" trend; greyed BG grounds the brights. Poor answer (random hues, no justification) reveals inability to synthesise theory with market context — a key NIFT/NID entrance skill.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Colour theory is the systematic study of how colours interact, combine, and affect human perception, organised through the colour wheel which arranges hues by wavelength ______.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're designing a festive kurta set for Diwali — your client wants something "______ but modern" that suits her wheatish complexion and doesn't look "too loud." Where do you start?
What is Colour theory? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Colour theory is the systematic study of how colours interact, combine, and affect human perception, organised through the colour wheel which arranges hues by wavelength relationships.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Colour theory?
questions.a: Students believe "complementary colours always look good together" and use them in equal proportions at full intensity (e.g., bright red + bright green kurta-pant).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) construct a 12-hue colour wheel labelling primary, secondary, and tertiary colours with correct angular positions, and (2) given a design brief (occasion, figure type, fabric), select and justify an appropriate colour scheme using hue, value, and intensity terminology with reference to the colour wheel.
